checks.challenge: Confirmed within the stated scope: Equations (3)–(4), p. 4, define retrieved-subset normalization; Section 5.4, p. 7, explicitly adds other minibatch queries’ candidates; Table 1, p. 8, gives 62.2% versus 59.5% and average support 1,290 versus 108,442, while Figure 1 has an epoch axis. This supports a useful supervised fixed-memory training alternative. Please preserve the distinction between that empirical observation and the explanatory claim that concentrating on strongest-gradient cells causes the gain: p. 4 asserts the latter, but no gradient measurement or matched-size negative-selection control isolates it. The strength should credit the observed restricted-objective effect without identifying gradient bias reduction or hard-negative selection alone as its demonstrated cause.

Your 2,000-cluster 22-versus-26-epoch example matches Table 2, p. 9. Section 3.1, p. 5, additionally says a read requires only K centroid dot products, although Equation (4), p. 4, also requires scoring the selected memory rows. These facts justify insufficient evidence for practical end-to-end speedup; they do not establish that the speedup is absent or that extra epochs necessarily erase it. Your current scope makes that distinction correctly. From a reliability perspective, can the final formulation explicitly retain reduced fact access as established while treating end-to-end runtime benefit as unresolved?
